This appendix collects the solutions of the exercises, chapter by chapter. It grows as the book grows: each new chapter adds its own section.

How to use it. Try the exercise first, then read the hint in the chapter, and only then look here. For the manual exercises the solution is written out in full. For the computational exercises the solution is a complete, executable piece of code, followed by a short discussion of what the output shows; there are many correct ways to write such code, and yours may differ.

A note on the code. Each solution lives in a function (solution_1_6(), and so on), so that the cells do not overwrite each other’s variables. The function names match the exercise numbers.

import platform
from importlib.metadata import version

print("Python", platform.python_version())
for pkg in ["numpy", "scipy", "pandas", "matplotlib", "scikit-learn"]:
    print(f"{pkg:<14}{version(pkg)}")



import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Solution 1.2 — Shapes.
(a) \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{200 \times 5} and \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{200}.
(b) The intercept column adds one column: 200 \times 6.
(c) \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} is d \times d, that is 5 \times 5 (and 6 \times 6 for the design matrix with the intercept). Its size depends on the number of features, not on the number of samples.
(d) Each entry of \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} is the dot product of a row of \mathbf{X} with \mathbf{w}:\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} = \begin{pmatrix} 1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot(-1) \\ 3\cdot 1 + 4\cdot(-1) \\ 5\cdot 1 + 6\cdot(-1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}.

The i-th entry is the prediction of the linear model f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} for the i-th sample; here, the first feature minus the second.

Solution 1.3 — Least squares by hand. The points are (0,2), (1,2), (2,5).

(a) \mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}. Then \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix} and \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}. With \det = 6,\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 5 & -3 \\ -3 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}
= \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3/2 \\ 3/2 \end{pmatrix},

so the line is \hat{y} = \tfrac32 + \tfrac32 x.

(b) \hat{\mathbf{y}} = (1.5,\ 3,\ 4.5)^\top, hence \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} = (0.5,\ -1,\ 0.5)^\top. Then \sum_i r_i = 0 and \mathbf{r}\cdot(0,1,2) = 0 - 1 + 1 = 0: \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}.

(c) \text{MSE} = \frac{0.25 + 1 + 0.25}{3} = 0.5. The mean of \mathbf{y} is 3 and \sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2 = 1 + 1 + 4 = 6, so R^2 = 1 - \frac{1.5}{6} = 0.75.

Solution 1.4 — Derive it yourself.
(a) L(w) = \sum_i (y_i - w x_i)^2, so L'(w) = -2\sum_i x_i (y_i - w x_i). Setting L'(w) = 0 gives \sum_i x_i y_i = w \sum_i x_i^2, that is\hat{w} = \frac{\sum_i x_i y_i}{\sum_i x_i^2}.

(b) With a single column \mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top as the data matrix, \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x} = \sum_i x_i^2 (a 1\times 1 matrix) and \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} = \sum_i x_i y_i, so (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} is the same ratio.

(c) L''(w) = 2\sum_i x_i^2, which is strictly positive unless every x_i is zero. Hence L is strictly convex and \hat{w} is its unique minimizer.

Solution 1.5 — Which loss, which constant?
(a) f(c) = \sum_i (y_i - c)^2 has f'(c) = -2\sum_i (y_i - c), which vanishes at c = \frac1n\sum_i y_i; and f'' = 2n > 0. The minimizer is the mean.

(b) Let g(c) = \sum_i \lvert y_i - c\rvert, with n = 2m - 1 and m = (n+1)/2. The function g is piecewise linear. At a point c that is not a data point, g'(c) = \#\{y_i < c\} - \#\{y_i > c\} (each term with y_i < c contributes +1, each term with y_i > c contributes -1).

For c between y_{(m-1)} and y_{(m)}: m - 1 points lie below and m above, so g' = -1 < 0.

For c between y_{(m)} and y_{(m+1)}: m points lie below and m - 1 above, so g' = +1 > 0.

More generally the slope is 2k - n when k points lie below c, which is negative for k < m and positive for k \ge m. So g decreases up to y_{(m)} and increases afterwards: the minimizer is y_{(m)}, the median.

(c) Replace y_n by 

106. The order of the points is unchanged (it was already the largest, and it only grows), so the median is unchanged. The mean instead moves by (10^6 - y_n)/n, which can be enormous: one outlier drags the optimal constant of the squared loss arbitrarily far. The squared loss is therefore sensitive to outliers (it squares large errors), while the absolute loss is robust. When the data may contain outliers, the choice of loss matters as much as the choice of model.

Solution 1.6 — Meet a new data set.

def solution_1_6():
    from sklearn.datasets import load_wine

    wine = load_wine(as_frame=True)
    X, y = wine.data, wine.target
    print("shape of X:", X.shape)
    print("classes:", dict(zip(wine.target_names.tolist(), np.bincount(y).tolist())))
    print("first five features:", X.columns[:5].tolist())

    stats = X.describe().loc[["mean", "std"]].T
    print("\nmean and standard deviation of each feature:")
    print(stats.round(3).to_string())
    print("\nfeature with the largest standard deviation:", stats["std"].idxmax())

solution_1_6()



The Wine data set has 178 samples, 13 features, and 3 classes. The feature proline lives on a scale of hundreds (its mean is in the 700s and its standard deviation above 300), while most other features are of order 1 to 100 and some are below 1. In a distance-based method such as k-NN, proline would dominate the Euclidean distance and the other features would barely matter: standardize the features first (Section 1.8).

Solution 1.7 — A line on Iris.

def solution_1_7():
    from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
    from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

    iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
    x = iris.data["petal length (cm)"].to_numpy()
    t = iris.data["petal width (cm)"].to_numpy()
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])

    # (a) three ways to the same answer
    w_normal = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ t)
    w_lstsq = np.linalg.lstsq(A, t, rcond=None)[0]
    lr = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), t)
    w_sk = np.array([lr.intercept_, lr.coef_[0]])
    print("normal equations:", w_normal.round(5))
    print("lstsq           :", w_lstsq.round(5))
    print("scikit-learn    :", w_sk.round(5))
    print("all agree:", np.allclose(w_normal, w_lstsq) and np.allclose(w_normal, w_sk))

    # (b) error, baseline, R^2
    t_hat = A @ w_normal
    mse = np.mean((t - t_hat) ** 2)
    mse_base = np.mean((t - t.mean()) ** 2)
    r2 = 1 - np.sum((t - t_hat) ** 2) / np.sum((t - t.mean()) ** 2)
    print(f"\nMSE = {mse:.4f} | baseline MSE = {mse_base:.4f} | R^2 = {r2:.4f}")

    # (c) plot
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.2))
    species = iris.target.to_numpy()
    for k, (name, color, marker) in enumerate(zip(iris.target_names, [BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN], ["o", "s", "^"])):
        ax.scatter(x[species == k], t[species == k], s=26, color=color, marker=marker,
                   edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4, label=name)
    xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 100)
    ax.plot(xs, w_normal[0] + w_normal[1] * xs, color="black", linewidth=2, label="least-squares line")
    ax.set_xlabel("petal length (cm)")
    ax.set_ylabel("petal width (cm)")
    ax.set_title("Iris: petal width as a linear function of petal length")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

solution_1_7()





The three methods agree to numerical precision. The line explains more than 90% of the variance of the petal width (compare the MSE with the baseline MSE, and read the R^2): on this data set the two petal measurements are strongly linearly related. Note that the cloud is not homogeneous across species, and the line is a compromise between the three groups.

Solution 1.8 — Does scaling matter?

def solution_1_8():
    from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
    from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
    from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
    from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
    from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

    X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
    ks = np.arange(1, 16)

    def test_accuracies(seed):
        X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
        raw = [KNeighborsClassifier(k).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te) for k in ks]
        scaled = [make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(k)).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te)
                  for k in ks]
        return raw, scaled

    # the split of Section 1.8 (random_state = SEED)
    raw_1, scaled_1 = test_accuracies(SEED)
    # ten different splits
    seeds = range(10)
    all_raw, all_scaled = map(np.array, zip(*(test_accuracies(s) for s in seeds)))

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), sharey=True)
    axes[0].plot(ks, raw_1, "o--", color=VERMILION, label="raw features")
    axes[0].plot(ks, scaled_1, "s-", color=BLUE, label="standardized")
    axes[0].set_title(f"One split (random_state={SEED})")
    axes[1].plot(ks, all_raw.mean(axis=0), "o--", color=VERMILION, label="raw features")
    axes[1].plot(ks, all_scaled.mean(axis=0), "s-", color=BLUE, label="standardized")
    axes[1].fill_between(ks, all_scaled.mean(0) - all_scaled.std(0), all_scaled.mean(0) + all_scaled.std(0),
                         color=BLUE, alpha=0.15)
    axes[1].fill_between(ks, all_raw.mean(0) - all_raw.std(0), all_raw.mean(0) + all_raw.std(0),
                         color=VERMILION, alpha=0.15)
    axes[1].set_title("Mean over 10 splits (band: ± 1 std across splits)")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_xlabel("number of neighbors k")
        ax.legend()
    axes[0].set_ylabel("test accuracy")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    diff = all_scaled - all_raw                      # shape (10 splits, 15 values of k)
    print(f"mean accuracy gain from scaling: {diff.mean():.3f}")
    print(f"fraction of (split, k) pairs where scaling is at least as good: {(diff >= 0).mean():.3f}")
    print(f"fraction where scaling is strictly better: {(diff > 0).mean():.3f}")

solution_1_8()





The conclusion is stable. Averaged over the ten splits, standardized features give a higher test accuracy for essentially every k (the gain is about three percentage points in our run), and the printed fractions show that scaling was never worse and almost always strictly better across all the (split, k) pairs. A single split would have been enough to see the effect here, but only repeating the experiment lets us say that the conclusion does not depend on the lucky choice of one split. This habit, repeating the evaluation on several splits, is formalized as cross-validation in Chapter 5.

Solution 1.9 — Your own overfitting experiment.

def solution_1_9():
    from numpy.polynomial import polynomial as P
    from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
    from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

    d = load_diabetes(as_frame=True, scaled=False)
    target = d.target.to_numpy()
    MAX_DEG, N_SPLITS = 8, 100

    def median_test_errors(z, n_train):
        errs = np.zeros((N_SPLITS, MAX_DEG + 1))
        for s in range(N_SPLITS):
            z_tr, z_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(z, target, train_size=n_train, random_state=s)
            for degree in range(MAX_DEG + 1):
                coef = P.polyfit(z_tr, y_tr, degree)
                errs[s, degree] = np.mean((y_te - P.polyval(z_te, coef)) ** 2)
        return np.median(errs, axis=0)

    rows = []
    for feature in ["bp", "s5"]:
        f = d.data[feature].to_numpy()
        z = (f - f.mean()) / f.std()
        for n_train in [30, 100, 300]:
            med = median_test_errors(z, n_train)
            rows.append({"feature": feature, "training size": n_train,
                         "best degree": int(med.argmin()),
                         "test MSE at best degree": round(float(med.min()), 0),
                         "test MSE at degree 1 (a line)": round(float(med[1]), 0),
                         "test MSE at degree 0 (baseline)": round(float(med[0]), 0)})
    print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

solution_1_9()



In the table, the best degree does not decrease as the training set grows, and it tends to increase: with 30 patients a straight line is the best choice for both features, while with 300 patients a slightly more flexible curve is preferred. The reason is that the variance of a flexible model comes from having too few samples to pin down its many coefficients; as n grows this variance shrinks, and the best compromise moves towards more flexibility. Note also that the gain of the best degree over a straight line is small (a few percent at most, and nil for bp with 100 or fewer patients): the relationship between a single feature and the target is weak and almost linear, so there is little to gain from flexibility, and the errors for neighboring degrees are close. Every model, however, is clearly better than the baseline (degree 0). The idea that the right complexity depends on the amount of data returns in Chapters 3 and 4.

Solution 1.10 — When \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} is singular.

def solution_1_10():
    from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes

    d = load_diabetes(as_frame=True, scaled=False)
    bmi, target = d.data["bmi"].to_numpy(), d.target.to_numpy()
    A1 = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(bmi), bmi])            # intercept + bmi
    A2 = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(bmi), bmi, bmi])       # intercept + bmi + a duplicate of bmi

    # (a) rank and conditioning
    print("rank of A1:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(A1), "| rank of A2:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(A2),
          "(A2 has 3 columns but only 2 independent ones)")
    print(f"condition number of A1^T A1: {np.linalg.cond(A1.T @ A1):.3g}")
    print(f"condition number of A2^T A2: {np.linalg.cond(A2.T @ A2):.3g}")

    # (b) the normal equations
    try:
        w_solve = np.linalg.solve(A2.T @ A2, A2.T @ target)
        print("np.linalg.solve returned (numerically meaningless):", w_solve)
    except np.linalg.LinAlgError as err:
        print("np.linalg.solve raised LinAlgError:", err)

    # (c) lstsq
    w2 = np.linalg.lstsq(A2, target, rcond=None)[0]
    w1 = np.linalg.lstsq(A1, target, rcond=None)[0]
    print("\nlstsq on A2:", w2.round(4), "| norm:", round(float(np.linalg.norm(w2)), 4))
    print("lstsq on A1:", w1.round(4))
    print("same predictions with and without the duplicate column:", np.allclose(A2 @ w2, A1 @ w1))

    # (d) other solutions with the same predictions
    candidates = {"(w1, 0)": np.array([w1[0], w1[1], 0.0]),
                  "(w1/2, w1/2)  [what lstsq picks]": np.array([w1[0], w1[1] / 2, w1[1] / 2]),
                  "(3 w1/4, w1/4)": np.array([w1[0], 0.75 * w1[1], 0.25 * w1[1]])}
    print("\nweights giving exactly the same predictions, and their norms:")
    for name, w in candidates.items():
        print(f"  {name:<36} predictions equal: {np.allclose(A2 @ w, A1 @ w1)} | norm = {np.linalg.norm(w):.4f}")

solution_1_10()



(a) The matrix \mathbf{A}_2 has three columns but rank 2, because the third column equals the second. Consequently \mathbf{A}_2^\top\mathbf{A}_2 is singular, and its condition number is astronomically large (of the order of the inverse of machine precision, or beyond), while that of \mathbf{A}_1^\top\mathbf{A}_1 is moderate.

(b) The normal equations no longer have a unique solution. Depending on rounding errors, np.linalg.solve either raises a LinAlgError (“Singular matrix”) or returns meaningless numbers; you must not rely on either behavior.

(c) np.linalg.lstsq works through the SVD and returns the solution of minimum norm among all least-squares solutions: it splits the coefficient of bmi equally between the two identical columns. The predictions are exactly those of the model that uses bmi once.

(d) In terms of the column space: adding a column that is already a linear combination of the others does not enlarge the column space, so the projection \hat{\mathbf{y}} is the same. What changes is the parametrization: infinitely many weight vectors (w_0, a, b) with a + b = w_1 produce the same \hat{\mathbf{y}}, and the normal equations are underdetermined. Ranking them by their norm, as lstsq does, picks one; regularization (Chapter 6) will do something similar in a principled way and will also make the problem well-conditioned.

(b) np.mean((y - X @ w) ** 2). The shapes are: X @ w is (n, d)\,@\,(d,) \to (n,); y - X @ w is (n,); the square is (n,); and the mean is a scalar, shape ().

(c) y - y_hat has shape (n, n): the vector y is treated as a row (1, n) and y_hat as a column, so the entry (i, j) is y_j - \hat y_i. The mean of the squares is the average of (y_j - \hat y_i)^2 over all pairs. Expanding the square and averaging over i and j gives\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i,j}(y_j - \hat y_i)^2 = \overline{y^2} - 2\,\bar y\,\bar{\hat y} + \overline{\hat y^2} = \operatorname{Var}(y) + \operatorname{Var}(\hat y) + (\bar y - \bar{\hat y})^2,

with the variances computed with the divisor n. It measures how different the distributions of the targets and of the predictions are, not how good each individual prediction is. On the data of the Pitfall, \bar y = 2.5, \bar{\hat y} = 2.75, \operatorname{Var}(y) = 1.25 and \operatorname{Var}(\hat y) = 1.1875, so the result is 1.25 + 1.1875 + 0.0625 = 2.5, which is the “wrong MSE” printed in Section 2.3.6, while the correct MSE is 0.25.

Solution 2.2 — Counting heads.

(a) \mathbb{P}(X = k) = \binom{3}{k}/8, that is \tfrac18, \tfrac38, \tfrac38, \tfrac18 for k = 0, 1, 2, 3.

(b) \mathbb{E}[X] = 0\cdot\tfrac18 + 1\cdot\tfrac38 + 2\cdot\tfrac38 + 3\cdot\tfrac18 = \tfrac{12}{8} = 1.5 = np. Moreover \mathbb{E}[X^2] = 0 + \tfrac38 + \tfrac{12}{8} + \tfrac98 = 3, so \operatorname{Var}(X) = 3 - 1.5^2 = 0.75 = np(1-p) = 3 \cdot \tfrac14.

(c) \mathbb{E}[Z] = 2 \cdot 1.5 - 3 = 0 and \operatorname{Var}(Z) = 2^2 \cdot 0.75 = 3. Since 3 - X is the number of tails, Z = X - (3 - X) is heads minus tails: the position, after three steps, of a walker that moves \pm 1 with equal probability. It is symmetric around 0.

Solution 2.3 — A spam filter by Bayes.

(a) With S = spam, \mathbb{P}(S) = 0.4, \mathbb{P}(\text{free}\mid S) = 0.6, \mathbb{P}(\text{free}\mid \bar S) = 0.05:\mathbb{P}(S \mid \text{free}) = \frac{0.6 \cdot 0.4}{0.6 \cdot 0.4 + 0.05 \cdot 0.6} = \frac{0.24}{0.27} = \frac{8}{9} \approx 0.889.

(b) Assuming that the two words are independent within each class,\mathbb{P}(S \mid \text{free}, \text{winner}) = \frac{0.4 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.3}{0.4 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.3 + 0.6 \cdot 0.05 \cdot 0.02} = \frac{0.072}{0.0726} \approx 0.992.

(c) The assumption is conditional independence given the class: \mathbb{P}(\text{free}, \text{winner}\mid S) = \mathbb{P}(\text{free}\mid S)\,\mathbb{P}(\text{winner}\mid S), and the same for ham. If the words are correlated inside a class (and in spam they probably are), the second word carries less new information than the product suggests, so the evidence is counted twice and the posterior tends to be overconfident. This is the “naive” assumption of the naive Bayes classifier: it is often wrong, yet the resulting classifier can still work well, because only the ranking of the classes matters.

Solution 2.4 — Maximum likelihood for the exponential distribution.

(a) \ell(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log(\lambda e^{-\lambda x_i}) = n\log\lambda - \lambda\sum_i x_i. Then \ell'(\lambda) = n/\lambda - \sum_i x_i = 0 gives\hat\lambda = \frac{n}{\sum_i x_i} = \frac{1}{\bar x}.

(b) \ell''(\lambda) = -n/\lambda^2 < 0 for every \lambda > 0: the log-likelihood is concave, so \hat\lambda is the maximum.

(c) \sum_i x_i = 5 and n = 4, so \bar x = 1.25 and \hat\lambda = 0.8. The mean of the fitted distribution is 1/\hat\lambda = 1.25, which is exactly the sample mean: for the exponential family, maximum likelihood matches the model’s mean with the data’s mean.

Solution 2.5 — Covariance matrices and whitening.

(a) \det(\boldsymbol\Sigma - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = (5 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda) - 4 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6 = (\lambda - 6)(\lambda - 1), so \lambda_1 = 6 and \lambda_2 = 1. For \lambda_1 = 6: (5 - 6)v_1 + 2v_2 = 0, so v_2 = v_1/2 and \mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(2, 1)^\top. For \lambda_2 = 1: 4v_1 + 2v_2 = 0, so \mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(1, -2)^\top (eigenvectors are defined up to a sign). The variance of \mathbf{x} is 6 along \mathbf{q}_1 (standard deviation \sqrt6 \approx 2.45) and 1 along \mathbf{q}_2.

(b) Using \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}] = \mathbf{0} and the linearity of expectation, \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}^\top] = \mathbf{A}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top]\,\mathbf{A}^\top = \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{A}^\top. (With a nonzero mean, apply the same steps to \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu.) For a vector \mathbf{v}, take \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{v}^\top: \mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{v} = \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{x}) \ge 0, because a variance is an expectation of a square. Hence \boldsymbol\Sigma is positive semidefinite.

(c) With \mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{q}_1\ \mathbf{q}_2) and \boldsymbol\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(6, 1), let \mathbf{A} = \boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1/2}\mathbf{Q}^\top. By (b),\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{A}^\top = \boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1/2}\mathbf{Q}^\top(\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf{Q}^\top)\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1/2} = \boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1/2}\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1/2} = \mathbf{I}.

Explicitly, \mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2/\sqrt{30} & 1/\sqrt{30} \\ 1/\sqrt5 & -2/\sqrt5 \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.365 & 0.183 \\ 0.447 & -0.894 \end{pmatrix}. The transformation rotates the axes onto the eigenvectors and divides each coordinate by its standard deviation: the elliptical cloud becomes a round one.

(d) Let \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}; then \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) and \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{z}^\top\mathbf{z} (the squared Mahalanobis distance is the ordinary squared distance after whitening). For two standard Gaussian coordinates, \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{z}^\top\mathbf{z} \le c^2) = 1 - e^{-c^2/2}, so with c^2 = 4 the probability is 1 - e^{-2} \approx 0.865.

The cell below checks (a), (c) and (d) numerically.

Sigma = np.array([[5.0, 2.0], [2.0, 2.0]])
lam, Q = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma)                     # eigenvalues in increasing order
lam, Q = lam[::-1], Q[:, ::-1]                     # decreasing order, as in the solution above
Q = Q * np.sign(Q[0, :])                           # sign convention: first component positive
print("eigenvalues:", lam, "| eigenvectors (columns):\n", Q.round(4))

A_white = np.diag(lam ** -0.5) @ Q.T
print("\nwhitening matrix A:\n", A_white.round(4))
print("A Sigma A^T = I:", np.allclose(A_white @ Sigma @ A_white.T, np.eye(2)))

x = np.random.default_rng(SEED).multivariate_normal([0, 0], Sigma, size=200_000)
d2 = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", x, np.linalg.inv(Sigma), x)
print(f"\nfraction with x^T Sigma^-1 x <= 4: {(d2 <= 4).mean():.4f}   theory 1 - exp(-2) = {1 - np.exp(-2):.4f}")
print("covariance of the whitened sample:\n", np.cov(x @ A_white.T, rowvar=False).round(3))

    from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

    iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
    frame, labels = iris.data, iris.target
    X, y = frame.to_numpy(), labels.to_numpy()

    means_mask = np.array([X[y == k].mean(axis=0) for k in range(3)])
    means_pandas = frame.groupby(labels).mean().to_numpy()
    print(pd.DataFrame(means_mask, index=iris.target_names, columns=frame.columns).round(3).to_string())
    print("agrees with pandas groupby:", np.allclose(means_mask, means_pandas))

    # (b) standardization with broadcasting
    Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)          # (150, 4) - (4,), then / (4,)
    print("\ncolumn means:", Z.mean(axis=0).round(10), "| column stds:", Z.std(axis=0).round(10))

    # (c) covariance of the standardized data = correlation matrix of the raw data
    cov_Z = np.cov(Z, rowvar=False, ddof=0)
    corr_X = np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False)
    print("cov(standardized) equals corr(raw):", np.allclose(cov_Z, corr_X))
    print(pd.DataFrame(corr_X, index=frame.columns, columns=frame.columns).round(2).to_string())

solution_2_6()



(a) The loop over the species with a Boolean mask gives the same table as groupby. (b) Subtracting the vector of means and dividing by the vector of standard deviations broadcasts over the 150 rows; the standardized columns have mean 0 (up to rounding) and standard deviation 1 (np.std divides by n, the convention of StandardScaler). (c) The covariance of two standardized variables is \operatorname{Cov}(x_i, x_j)/(\sigma_i\sigma_j), which is by definition their correlation \rho_{ij}: standardizing turns the covariance matrix into the correlation matrix. (Both must use the same divisor, which is why we pass ddof=0; with ddof=1 the covariance matrix would be larger by the factor n/(n-1).) The strong positive correlation between petal length and petal width, about 0.96, and the negative correlation between sepal width and the petal measurements are visible in the table.

def solution_2_7():
    from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
    from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
    from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
    from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

    def knn_predict(X_train, y_train, X_test, k=5):
        # squared distances between all test and training points, shape (n_test, n_train)
        sq_train, sq_test = (X_train ** 2).sum(axis=1), (X_test ** 2).sum(axis=1)
        D2 = sq_test[:, None] + sq_train[None, :] - 2 * X_test @ X_train.T
        nearest = np.argpartition(D2, k - 1, axis=1)[:, :k]          # indices of the k smallest distances in each row
        votes = y_train[nearest]                                      # labels of the neighbors, shape (n_test, k)
        return np.array([np.bincount(row).argmax() for row in votes])  # majority vote (ties go to the smallest label)

    X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
    agreement, acc_mine, acc_sklearn = [], [], []
    for seed in range(30):
        X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
        scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_tr)
        Z_tr, Z_te = scaler.transform(X_tr), scaler.transform(X_te)
        mine = knn_predict(Z_tr, y_tr, Z_te, k=5)
        reference = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5).fit(Z_tr, y_tr).predict(Z_te)
        agreement.append((mine == reference).mean())
        acc_mine.append((mine == y_te).mean())
        acc_sklearn.append((reference == y_te).mean())

    print(f"agreement with scikit-learn over 30 splits: mean {np.mean(agreement):.4f}, minimum {np.min(agreement):.4f}")
    print(f"mean test accuracy: ours {np.mean(acc_mine):.3f} | scikit-learn {np.mean(acc_sklearn):.3f}")

solution_2_7()



The two classifiers make the same predictions on every test point of every split. The only loop is the one that counts the votes of each test point; the expensive part, the distances between all pairs, is a single matrix product (the Gram identity of Worked example 2.1). The accuracy of about 0.96 is the same as in Section 2.7.1, as it should be. With ties between distances or between votes the two implementations could in principle differ, but with continuous features they are rare.

def solution_2_8():
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

    bc = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
    df = bc.frame
    X, t = df.drop(columns="target"), df["target"]

    # (a) classes
    print("target names (index = code):", dict(enumerate(bc.target_names.tolist())))
    print("samples per class:", t.value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())

    # (b) standardized difference between the class means (pooled standard deviation)
    n0, n1 = (t == 0).sum(), (t == 1).sum()
    m0, m1 = X[t == 0].mean(), X[t == 1].mean()
    pooled = np.sqrt(((n0 - 1) * X[t == 0].var() + (n1 - 1) * X[t == 1].var()) / (n0 + n1 - 2))
    d = ((m0 - m1).abs() / pooled).sort_values(ascending=False)
    print("\nfive best separating features:")
    print(d.head(5).round(2).to_string())
    print("\nthree worst:")
    print(d.tail(3).round(2).to_string())

    # (c) scatter plot of the two best features
    f1, f2 = d.index[:2]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.4))
    for code, color, marker in [(0, VERMILION, "o"), (1, BLUE, "s")]:
        sel = t == code
        ax.scatter(X.loc[sel, f1], X.loc[sel, f2], s=18, color=color, marker=marker, alpha=0.7, label=bc.target_names[code])
    ax.set(xlabel=f1, ylabel=f2, title="The two best separating features")
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # (d) redundancy between two features
    print(f"\ncorrelation of 'mean radius' and 'mean perimeter': {df['mean radius'].corr(df['mean perimeter']):.4f}")

solution_2_8()







(a) The data set has 212 malignant tumors (code 0) and 357 benign ones (code 1). (b) The features describing the “worst” (largest) values of the concave points, the perimeter, and the radius, together with the mean concave points, separate the classes best: the class means differ by 2.5 to 2.7 pooled standard deviations, and the mean perimeter is fifth with 2.3. The worst features, the symmetry error, the texture error, and the mean fractal dimension, have a difference of at most 0.03 pooled standard deviations: the two classes look the same in these variables, taken one at a time. (c) In the scatter plot the two classes form two clouds with only a small overlap. (d) The correlation between mean radius and mean perimeter is 0.998: the perimeter of a nearly round tumor is just 2\pi times its radius, so the two columns carry the same information. A linear model with both features has almost linearly dependent columns (Exercise 1.10): the weights become unstable and hard to interpret, which is one of the reasons for the regularization of Chapter 6 and the feature selection of Chapter 10.

def solution_2_9():
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    from scipy import stats

    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    reps, ns = 200_000, [1, 2, 3, 5, 10]
    uniform = rng.random((reps, max(ns)))                 # mean 1/2, standard deviation sqrt(1/12)
    exponential = rng.exponential(1.0, size=(reps, max(ns)))   # mean 1, standard deviation 1

    def ks_distance(samples, mu, sigma, n):
        z = (samples[:, :n].mean(axis=1) - mu) * np.sqrt(n) / sigma
        return stats.kstest(z, "norm").statistic

    ks_uniform = np.array([ks_distance(uniform, 0.5, np.sqrt(1 / 12), n) for n in ns])
    ks_expon = np.array([ks_distance(exponential, 1.0, 1.0, n) for n in ns])

    print(f"{'n':>3} {'uniform':>9} {'exponential':>12}")
    for n, a, b in zip(ns, ks_uniform, ks_expon):
        print(f"{n:>3} {a:>9.4f} {b:>12.4f}")
    slope_u = np.polyfit(np.log(ns), np.log(ks_uniform), 1)[0]
    slope_e = np.polyfit(np.log(ns), np.log(ks_expon), 1)[0]
    print(f"\nslope of log(KS) against log(n): uniform {slope_u:.2f}, exponential {slope_e:.2f}")

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.2))
    ax.loglog(ns, ks_uniform, "s-", color=BLUE, label="uniform (skewness 0)")
    ax.loglog(ns, ks_expon, "o--", color=ORANGE, label="exponential (skewness 2)")
    grid = np.array(ns, dtype=float)
    ax.loglog(grid, 0.16 / np.sqrt(grid), ":", color="gray", label=r"$\propto 1/\sqrt{n}$")
    ax.loglog(grid, 0.06 / grid, "-.", color="gray", label=r"$\propto 1/n$")
    ax.set(xlabel="n", ylabel="Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance to N(0, 1)", title="How fast is the central limit theorem?")
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

solution_2_9()





The distance to the Gaussian shrinks for both distributions, but at different speeds: the slope on the log-log plot is about -0.54 for the exponential distribution (close to the -1/2 of an error proportional to 1/\sqrt{n}) and about -1.2 for the uniform one, whose error shrinks like 1/n (the fitted slopes are estimates, and for the uniform at n = 10 the distance, about 0.003, is already close to the noise level of the experiment, of the order of 1/\sqrt{200{,}000}). The explanation is the skewness. The leading error term in the central limit theorem is proportional to the skewness of the original distribution divided by \sqrt{n}. The exponential distribution is strongly skewed (skewness 2), so this term is present; the uniform distribution is symmetric (skewness 0), the term vanishes, and the next one, of order 1/n, dominates. In practice: for symmetric, light-tailed data the Gaussian approximation of an average is excellent already with a handful of samples; for skewed or heavy-tailed data it needs many more.

def solution_2_10():
    from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
    from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
    from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
    from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
    from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
    from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler

    X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
    seeds = range(30)

    # (a) scalers and k
    def mean_accuracy(make_model, k):
        scores = []
        for seed in seeds:
            X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
            scores.append(make_model(k).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te))
        return np.mean(scores)

    makers = {
        "no scaling":      lambda k: KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k),
        "standardization": lambda k: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)),
        "min-max":         lambda k: make_pipeline(MinMaxScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)),
        "robust":          lambda k: make_pipeline(RobustScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)),
    }
    table = pd.DataFrame({name: {f"k = {k}": mean_accuracy(maker, k) for k in (1, 5, 15)} for name, maker in makers.items()})
    print("(a) mean test accuracy over 30 splits:")
    print(table.round(3).to_string())

    # (b) leakage through the scaler
    print("\n(b) scaling the whole data set before splitting (leak) against the pipeline:")
    X_scaled_all = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)                  # the mistake: statistics of the test samples are used
    for k in (1, 5, 15):
        diffs, leak_scores, ok_scores = [], [], []
        for seed in seeds:
            X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
            Z_tr, Z_te, _, _ = train_test_split(X_scaled_all, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
            leak = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k).fit(Z_tr, y_tr).score(Z_te, y_te)
            ok = makers["standardization"](k).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te)
            leak_scores.append(leak); ok_scores.append(ok); diffs.append(leak - ok)
        print(f"  k = {k:>2}: leak {np.mean(leak_scores):.4f} | pipeline {np.mean(ok_scores):.4f} | "
              f"difference {np.mean(diffs):+.4f} (std over splits {np.std(diffs):.4f})")

    # (c) leakage through label-based feature selection, on pure noise
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    leak_scores, ok_scores = [], []
    for rep in range(30):
        X_noise = rng.normal(size=(60, 2000))
        y_noise = rng.integers(0, 2, size=60)                          # random labels: nothing can be learned
        X_sel = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=10).fit_transform(X_noise, y_noise)     # the mistake: selection sees all labels
        X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X_sel, y_noise, test_size=0.3, random_state=rep)
        leak_scores.append(KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te))
        X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X_noise, y_noise, test_size=0.3, random_state=rep)
        pipe = make_pipeline(SelectKBest(f_classif, k=10), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5))
        ok_scores.append(pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te))
    print("\n(c) pure noise, selection of 10 features out of 2000, 5-NN, 30 repetitions:")
    print(f"  selection before the split (leak): accuracy {np.mean(leak_scores):.3f} +/- {np.std(leak_scores):.3f}")
    print(f"  selection inside the pipeline    : accuracy {np.mean(ok_scores):.3f} +/- {np.std(ok_scores):.3f}")

solution_2_10()







(a) Without scaling the accuracy is about 0.70 to 0.73; with any of the three scalers it is about 0.95 to 0.97. Standardization and min-max scaling are practically equivalent on this data set (min-max is slightly better for k = 15), and the robust scaler is a bit behind. The best k depends on the scaler, which is a first hint that k must be tuned (Chapter 5).

(b) Scaling the whole data set before the split gives results that differ from the correct pipeline by about 0.001 or less on average, with a standard deviation over the splits of about 0.01 (for k = 1 the accuracies are even identical on every split): the difference is not systematic, it is lost in the noise. The reason is that the mean and standard deviation of 178 samples hardly change when 30% of the samples are left out: a scaler learns very little from the data. This is why leakage through scalers often goes unnoticed. It would be a mistake to conclude that the rule is unimportant.

(c) On random labels no method can be better than chance, so the correct accuracy is 0.5, and the pipeline indeed gives about 0.52. The “leaky” procedure reaches about 0.82: among 2000 random features, some happen to correlate with the random labels of the whole data set, test samples included, and keeping the ten best of them builds the test labels into the features. The model seems to have found real structure and has found none. The more the preprocessing step learns, in particular when it uses the labels, the larger the leak: every step that is fitted must be inside the pipeline.

The book follows one rule: all computation happens on your computer, never on a server. chapters/chXX_name.py          you write/edit the notebook as a plain text file (percent format)
          │
          │   python tools/book.py execute      (jupytext runs every cell, on your computer)
          ▼
 chapters/chXX_name.ipynb       the same notebook, now with all outputs and figures stored inside
          │
          │   python tools/book.py build        (Jupyter Book turns notebooks into HTML; it does NOT run code)
          ▼
 _build/html/                   a folder of static web pages
          │
          │   python tools/book.py publish      (pushes the folder to the gh-pages branch)
          ▼
 GitHub Pages                   serves the files as they are: nothing is computed there

Three facts make this work:

A Jupyter notebook (.ipynb) is a file that can store its outputs. After execute, the numbers, tables, and figures you see in the book are inside the file.

Jupyter Book 2 does not execute notebooks when it builds the site, unless you pass the --execute flag. It simply displays the stored outputs. The build script never passes that flag.

GitHub Pages can serve a branch of static files (gh-pages). We push the finished HTML there ourselves, so no workflow has to install Python or run notebooks on GitHub’s machines.

records.content:
On GitHub, create a public, empty repository named machine-learning-with-python-book under your account (without README or license, since they already exist locally).

Connect your local copy and upload the sources:git remote add origin https://github.com/Brosss98/machine-learning-with-python-book.git
git push -u origin main

(If you work on a fork or with another repository name, set the environment variable BOOK_BASE_URL=/your-repository-name before building. For a repository called username.github.io the base URL is empty.)

Build and publish the first time:python tools/book.py build --strict
python tools/book.py publish

The publish command runs ghp-import -n -p -f _build/html: it copies the contents of _build/html to the branch gh-pages (adding an empty .nojekyll file, which tells GitHub not to run any site generator) and pushes it.

On GitHub, open Settings → Pages. Under Build and deployment, choose Source: Deploy from a branch, then Branch: gh-pages, folder / (root), and save.

After a minute or two the book is online at 

https://​brosss98​.github​.io​/machine​-learning​-with​-python​-book/.

What “no computation on GitHub” means

No GitHub Actions workflow of this project installs Python, executes notebooks, or builds the site: you do all of that locally. When you push to gh-pages, GitHub runs its own built-in step that simply copies the files to its web servers. Because of .nojekyll, nothing is generated or executed. The pages online are therefore byte for byte the ones you checked on your computer.

Do not use jupyter book init --gh-pages: it creates a workflow that builds the site on GitHub’s machines, which is the opposite of what we want here.

Every new chapter is a small release. A typical session looks like this:# 1. write or edit chapters/chNN_name.py, and add the notebook to the toc in myst.yml
python tools/book.py execute                     # run the new/changed notebooks
python tools/book.py build --local --strict      # build and check locally
python tools/book.py serve                       # look at it in the browser, then Ctrl+C

# 2. new version number (this updates the cover, the copyright page, and CITATION.cff)
python tools/book.py set-version 0.2.0

# 3. save the sources and tag the release
git add -A
git commit -m "Add Chapter 2; release v0.2.0"
git tag v0.2.0
git push origin main --tags

# 4. build for GitHub Pages and publish
python tools/book.py build --strict
python tools/book.py publish

Versions follow the pattern MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: in this book each published chapter raises the minor number (0.1.0 → 0.2.0 → …), corrections raise the patch number (0.2.1), and 1.0.0 is the complete book. When you release 1.0.0, also remove the words “work in progress” from front_matter/index.md, front_matter/copyright.md, and README.md.

Symptom

Likely cause and remedy

jupytext or jupyter-book is “not found”

The environment is not active, or the packages are not installed. Activate it and run pip install -r requirements.txt.

Jupyter Book asks to install Node.js

Answer y, or install Node.js yourself, or use the conda environment.

The published site has no styles or images

The base URL does not match the repository name. Check the name, set BOOK_BASE_URL=/your-repository-name, and build and publish again.

The page shows a 404 error

GitHub Pages is not set to the gh-pages branch (step 4), or you must wait a few minutes after the first publication.

The book shows old outputs

The notebook was not executed again: run python tools/book.py execute (the build prints a warning for notebooks that are out of date).

A cell fails during execute

Read the error shown by jupytext; fix the cell and run execute again. The .ipynb of a failing notebook is not updated.

ValueError: No kernel found that matches the current python executable during execute

The environment is not registered as a Jupyter kernel. Run python tools/book.py setup-kernel once (with the environment active) and run execute again.

On the website, an empty box appears above the chapter title and the title is shown twice

The .ipynb starts with a stray cell, so Jupyter Book cannot use the first heading as the page title. Run python tools/book.py execute --force: it removes such cells and prints the first cell of each notebook, which must be a markdown cell starting with # .

“Kernel not found” or ModuleNotFoundError in JupyterLab

JupyterLab was started outside the environment. Activate the environment and start jupyter lab from there.

You want to rebuild everything from scratch

Delete the folder _build/ and build again.

The packages are listed in requirements.txt with lower bounds. To record the exact versions you used, run pip freeze > requirements-lock.txt and keep that file with your copy.

Every notebook uses a fixed random seed. Results that depend on random numbers should therefore be identical on your machine, up to small differences due to library versions or hardware.

All notebooks are designed to run on an ordinary laptop CPU; a GPU is never required.
From examples to predictions, and how to set up your workshop

The next two cells print the versions of the libraries used to produce the outputs you see in this page, and define the plotting style and the random seed used throughout the book. If you run the notebook yourself and your versions differ slightly, small numerical differences in the printed results are normal.

import platform
from importlib.metadata import version

print("Python", platform.python_version())
for pkg in ["numpy", "scipy", "pandas", "matplotlib", "seaborn", "scikit-learn"]:
    print(f"{pkg:<14}{version(pkg)}")



import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

SEED = 42  # fixed seed: random operations give the same result every time

# Plotting style used throughout the book.
# Colors from the Okabe-Ito palette, designed to stay distinguishable
# for readers with color-vision deficiencies.
BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN = "#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73"
VERMILION, SKY, PURPLE = "#D55E00", "#56B4E9", "#CC79A7"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 110,
    "figure.figsize": (6.4, 4.0),
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.alpha": 0.25,
    "font.size": 11,
    "axes.titlesize": 12,
    "axes.labelsize": 11,
})

Most programs you have written follow rules that a human wrote down: “if the input is negative, return an error”, “sort the list with this procedure”. This works when we can describe the rules. It fails for tasks such as recognizing a handwritten digit, flagging a spam message, or estimating how a patient’s condition will evolve: nobody can write down the rules, but we can easily collect examples.

Machine learning replaces “write the rules” with “show examples and let an algorithm find the rules”. A classical way to say this, due to Tom Mitchell, is the following. A program learns from experience E with respect to a task T and a performance measure P if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.



Spam filter

Diagnosis support

Task T

label a message as spam or not

label a tumor as benign or malignant

Experience E

messages already labeled by users

patient records with a confirmed diagnosis

Performance P

fraction of new messages labeled correctly

fraction of new patients labeled correctly

Key idea

Learning means improving performance on new data by using past data. A program that only memorizes its examples has not learned anything useful.

The kind of experience we have decides the kind of problem:

Paradigm

What the data looks like

Typical goal

Where in this book

Supervised learning

inputs \mathbf{x} with the desired outputs y

predict y for a new \mathbf{x}

Parts I–II and most of Part IV

Unsupervised learning

inputs \mathbf{x} only

discover structure: groups, directions of variation

Part III, autoencoders (Chapter 20)

Reinforcement learning

an agent acting in an environment and receiving rewards

choose actions that maximize the total reward

Chapter 22

Supervised learning has two main flavors, depending on the output:

regression: y is a real number (the price of a house, the progression of a disease);

classification: y is one of a finite number of classes (spam / not spam, the species of a flower, a digit from 0 to 9).

(Mixed settings, such as semi-supervised learning, where only some examples have labels, are discussed in Chapter 12.)

hierarchy.lvl2: 1.3 Anatomy of a supervised learning problem
1.3 Anatomy of a supervised learning problem

records.content:
Every supervised method in this book is built from the same five ingredients.

Data. A training set S = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n} of n examples. Each \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d lists d measurable properties (the features), and y_i is the target (or label).

Model. A family of candidate functions f(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}) that map an input to a prediction \hat{y}. The vector \mathbf{w} collects the parameters that the algorithm will choose.

Loss. A function \ell(y, \hat{y}) \ge 0 that measures how wrong a prediction is.

Learning algorithm. A procedure that chooses \mathbf{w} so that the average loss on the training set is small: this is an optimization problem.

Evaluation. A way to estimate how well the chosen model will do on new data.

A word on vocabulary: the same objects go by many names. Rows are called samples, examples, or observations; columns are features, predictors, or covariates; y is the target, label, or response. We also distinguish parameters (learned by the algorithm from the data, such as \mathbf{w}) from hyperparameters (chosen by you before training, such as the number of neighbors in k-NN or the strength of a regularizer). Chapter 5 is devoted to choosing hyperparameters well.

Here is where linear algebra enters. Stack the n input vectors as rows of a matrix:\mathbf{X} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_1^\top \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{x}_n^\top
\end{pmatrix}
\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d},
\qquad
\mathbf{y} =
\begin{pmatrix}
y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n
\end{pmatrix}
\in \mathbb{R}^{n}.

Each row of \mathbf{X} is one sample, i.e. a point in \mathbb{R}^d. Each column is one feature measured on all samples. This is exactly the convention of NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn: X has shape (n_samples, n_features).

Our first dataset is the famous Iris data set, collected by the botanist Edgar Anderson and made known to statisticians by R. A. Fisher (1936). It contains 150 flowers from 3 species of iris, each described by 4 measurements in centimeters. It is bundled with scikit-learn, so no download is needed.

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)          # as_frame=True gives pandas objects
X_iris = iris.data.to_numpy()            # the data matrix X, shape (n, d)
y_iris = iris.target.to_numpy()          # the targets y, integers 0, 1, 2

print("X shape:", X_iris.shape, "-> n =", X_iris.shape[0], "samples, d =", X_iris.shape[1], "features")
print("y shape:", y_iris.shape)
print("features:", list(iris.data.columns))
print("classes :", iris.target_names.tolist())



iris.data.head()   # the first five rows of X



Because each sample is a point of \mathbb{R}^4, we can use geometry. The Euclidean distance between two samples is\lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j \rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{d} (x_{ik} - x_{jk})^2},

and flowers of the same species should be closer to each other than flowers of different species. This simple idea, “similar inputs have similar outputs”, is the basis of many algorithms.

records.content:
Take sample 0 and sample 1 of the data set (both setosa), and sample 100 (virginica). Their coordinates, in the order (sepal length, sepal width, petal length, petal width), are\mathbf{x}_0 = (5.1,\ 3.5,\ 1.4,\ 0.2), \quad
\mathbf{x}_1 = (4.9,\ 3.0,\ 1.4,\ 0.2), \quad
\mathbf{x}_{100} = (6.3,\ 3.3,\ 6.0,\ 2.5).

Step 1. \mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}_1 = (0.2,\ 0.5,\ 0,\ 0), so
\lVert \mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}_1 \rVert_2 = \sqrt{0.04 + 0.25} = \sqrt{0.29} \approx 0.539.

Step 2. \mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}_{100} = (-1.2,\ 0.2,\ -4.6,\ -2.3), so
\lVert \mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}_{100} \rVert_2 = \sqrt{1.44 + 0.04 + 21.16 + 5.29} = \sqrt{27.93} \approx 5.285.

The two setosa flowers are about ten times closer to each other than a setosa is to a virginica. Let us check with NumPy.

x0, x1, x100 = X_iris[0], X_iris[1], X_iris[100]
print("x0   =", x0)
print("x1   =", x1)
print("x100 =", x100)
print("distance(x0, x1)   =", round(float(np.linalg.norm(x0 - x1)), 4))
print("distance(x0, x100) =", round(float(np.linalg.norm(x0 - x100)), 4))

records.content:
We cannot draw \mathbb{R}^4, but we can look at two features at a time. The code below is self-contained: you can copy it into a script and run it as it is. Species are encoded by color and by marker shape, so the figure stays readable in black and white.

# Figure 1.1 — two views of the Iris data set
# (the figure code lives in a function, so that it does not overwrite
#  variables of the notebook such as X, y or w)
def figure_1_1():
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

    iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
    data, target = iris.data, iris.target
    colors = [BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN]
    markers = ["o", "s", "^"]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
    views = [("sepal length (cm)", "sepal width (cm)"), ("petal length (cm)", "petal width (cm)")]
    for ax, (fx, fy) in zip(axes, views):
        for k, name in enumerate(iris.target_names):
            mask = target == k
            ax.scatter(data.loc[mask, fx], data.loc[mask, fy], s=28, c=colors[k],
                       marker=markers[k], alpha=0.85, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4, label=name)
        ax.set_xlabel(fx)
        ax.set_ylabel(fy)
    handles, labels = axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
    fig.legend(handles, labels, title="species", loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False)
    axes[0].set_title("Sepals: the species overlap")
    axes[1].set_title("Petals: the species separate")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.12, 1, 1))
    plt.show()

figure_1_1()



The petal measurements separate the three species much better than the sepal ones. A learning algorithm has to discover such facts from the data, usually in dimensions where we cannot draw a picture.

hierarchy.lvl3: Our very first learner: the nearest class mean
Our very first learner: the nearest class mean

records.content:
To make the vocabulary model, fit, predict concrete, here is a learner that needs only a mean.

Fit. For each class c, compute the mean \boldsymbol{\mu}_c of the training samples of that class. The parameters of the model are these class means.

Predict. Given a new \mathbf{x}, return the class whose mean is closest: \hat{y} = \operatorname{argmin}_c \lVert \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_c \rVert_2.

We train it on part of the data and test it on the rest. (Why we split the data is explained in Section 1.7; for the moment, accept that the test samples play the role of “new” flowers.)

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X_iris, y_iris, test_size=0.3, stratify=y_iris, random_state=SEED
)
print("training samples:", X_tr.shape[0], "| test samples:", X_te.shape[0])

# FIT: one mean vector per class -> a 3 x 4 matrix of parameters
class_means = np.vstack([X_tr[y_tr == c].mean(axis=0) for c in range(3)])
print("class means (rows = classes):")
print(class_means.round(3))

# PREDICT: distance from every test sample to every class mean, then argmin
diffs = X_te[:, None, :] - class_means[None, :, :]      # shape (n_test, 3, 4)
distances = np.linalg.norm(diffs, axis=2)               # shape (n_test, 3)
y_pred = distances.argmin(axis=1)

print("test accuracy:", round(float(np.mean(y_pred == y_te)), 3))



Roughly nine flowers out of ten are labeled correctly by a model made of twelve numbers. This is a very simple learner, yet it already has every ingredient of Section 1.3.

Try it

Change test_size or random_state in the split above and re-run the two cells. How much does the accuracy move? We will come back to this variability in Chapter 5.

hierarchy.lvl2: 1.5 Learning as optimization: losses and baselines
1.5 Learning as optimization: losses and baselines

records.content:
How do we say that a model is “good”? We choose a loss function \ell(y, \hat{y}) that scores one prediction, and we average it over the training set. For regression, the most common choices are\ell_{\text{sq}}(y, \hat{y}) = (y - \hat{y})^2 \quad \text{(squared loss)},
\qquad
\ell_{\text{abs}}(y, \hat{y}) = \lvert y - \hat{y} \rvert \quad \text{(absolute loss)},

and for classification the 0–1 loss, \ell_{0\text{-}1}(y, \hat{y}) = \mathbb{I}[y \neq \hat{y}], which counts mistakes. The average loss on the training set is the empirical risk\hat{R}_S(f) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell\bigl(y_i,\, f(\mathbf{x}_i)\bigr).

With the squared loss, \hat{R}_S(f) is the mean squared error (MSE). Learning then means: among the functions of the model family, find the one with the smallest empirical risk,\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf{w}} \ \hat{R}_S\bigl(f(\cdot\,; \mathbf{w})\bigr).

This principle is called empirical risk minimization; Chapter 3 studies when and why it works.

hierarchy.lvl2: 1.5 Learning as optimization: losses and baselines
1.5 Learning as optimization: losses and baselines

records.content:
Before building anything clever, ask: how well can we do while ignoring the input? Let the model be a constant, f(\mathbf{x}) = c. With the squared loss we want\min_{c} \ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - c)^2 .

The derivative with respect to c is -\frac{2}{n}\sum_i (y_i - c). Setting it to zero gives c = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i = \bar{y}: the best constant predictor under the squared loss is the sample mean, and its MSE is the (population) variance of y.

This baseline is more useful than it looks. Any serious model must beat it, otherwise the inputs are not helping. The coefficient of determination measures the improvement over this baseline:R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2}.

R^2 = 0 means “no better than the mean”, R^2 = 1 means perfect predictions (on the data used to compute it).

records.content:
We use the Diabetes data set bundled with scikit-learn (Efron, Hastie, Johnstone and Tibshirani, 2004): 442 patients, ten baseline measurements (age, sex, body mass index bmi, average blood pressure bp, and six blood serum measurements s1–s6), and a quantitative measure of disease progression one year later, which is our target y. By default scikit-learn returns the features already centered and rescaled; we ask for the original units with scaled=False, so that the numbers are easier to interpret.

from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes

diab = load_diabetes(as_frame=True, scaled=False)
X_diab, y_diab = diab.data, diab.target
print("shape of X:", X_diab.shape, "| shape of y:", y_diab.shape)
X_diab.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(2).T





# The best constant predictor and its MSE (the baseline)
y = y_diab.to_numpy()
y_mean = y.mean()
mse_baseline = np.mean((y - y_mean) ** 2)

print(f"mean of y            : {y_mean:.2f}")
print(f"MSE of the baseline  : {mse_baseline:.2f}")
print(f"variance of y (ddof=0): {np.var(y):.2f}   <- the same number, as the theory says")

# Check numerically that no other constant does better
candidates = np.linspace(y.min(), y.max(), 2001)
mse_curve = np.array([np.mean((y - c) ** 2) for c in candidates])
print(f"best constant on a grid: {candidates[mse_curve.argmin()]:.1f}")

hierarchy.lvl2: 1.6 Our first real learner: least squares
1.6 Our first real learner: least squares

records.content:
A constant ignores the inputs. The next step up is a linear model:f(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}, b) = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = w_1 x_1 + \dots + w_d x_d + b .

The intercept b can be absorbed into the weights by adding a constant feature equal to 1 to every sample. From now on, in this section, \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p} denotes the data matrix including a leading column of ones (so p = d + 1) and \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^p contains b as its first entry. All predictions at once are then \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}.

hierarchy.lvl2: 1.6 Our first real learner: least squares
1.6 Our first real learner: least squares

records.content:
With the squared loss, learning means minimizingL(\mathbf{w}) = \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} \rVert_2^2
= (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w})^\top (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}).

(This is n times the MSE; the factor n does not change the minimizer.)

Step 1: expand. Using (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w})^\top = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top and the fact that the scalar \mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} equals its own transpose \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}:L(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{y} - 2\,\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\,\mathbf{w}.

Step 2: differentiate. For a vector \mathbf{a} and a symmetric matrix \mathbf{A} we have \nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\,(\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{a} and \nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\,(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}) = 2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}. Hence\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L(\mathbf{w}) = -2\,\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y} + 2\,\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\,\mathbf{w}.

Step 3: set the gradient to zero. We obtain the normal equations\boxed{\ \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\,\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}\ }

If the columns of \mathbf{X} are linearly independent, \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} is invertible and \hat{\mathbf{w}} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}.

Why this is a minimum. The Hessian of L is 2\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}, which is positive semidefinite because \mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v} = \lVert \mathbf{X}\mathbf{v} \rVert_2^2 \ge 0. So L is convex and any solution of the normal equations is a global minimizer.

hierarchy.lvl2: 1.6 Our first real learner: least squares
1.6 Our first real learner: least squares

records.content:
The vectors \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}, as \mathbf{w} varies, fill the column space of \mathbf{X}, a subspace of \mathbb{R}^n. Least squares looks for the point of this subspace closest to \mathbf{y}, which is the orthogonal projection of \mathbf{y} onto it. Writing the residual as \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{w}}, the normal equations say exactly\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0},

that is, the residual is orthogonal to every column of \mathbf{X} (hence the name “normal”). The prediction vector is \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y} with the projection (“hat”) matrix \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top. Since the first column of \mathbf{X} is all ones, the first normal equation reads \sum_i r_i = 0: with an intercept, the residuals always sum to zero.

Key idea

Linear least squares is nothing more than an orthogonal projection. The “learning algorithm” is a linear-algebra computation, and the quality of the fit is the length of the part of \mathbf{y} that the columns of \mathbf{X} cannot reach.

hierarchy.lvl3: Worked example 1.2 — three points by hand
hierarchy.lvl2: 1.6 Our first real learner: least squares

hierarchy.lvl3: Worked example 1.2 — three points by hand
hierarchy.lvl2: 1.6 Our first real learner: least squares

records.content:
Fit a line y = w_0 + w_1 x to the three points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 4). Here\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}.

Step 1: the normal equations.\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 11 \end{pmatrix}.

Step 2: solve. \det(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}) = 15 - 9 = 6, so\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 5 & -3 \\ -3 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 11 \end{pmatrix}
= \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 7/6 \\ 3/2 \end{pmatrix}.

The fitted line is \hat{y} = \tfrac{7}{6} + \tfrac{3}{2}x.

Step 3: predictions and residuals. \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \bigl(\tfrac{7}{6},\ \tfrac{8}{3},\ \tfrac{25}{6}\bigr)^\top and \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \bigl(-\tfrac16,\ \tfrac13,\ -\tfrac16\bigr)^\top.

Step 4: check orthogonality. The sum of the residuals is -\tfrac16 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac16 = 0, and \mathbf{r}\cdot(0,1,2) = 0 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac13 = 0. Both columns of \mathbf{X} are orthogonal to \mathbf{r}, as the theory predicts.

Step 5: error and R^2. \sum_i r_i^2 = \tfrac{1}{36} + \tfrac{4}{36} + \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac16, so the MSE is \tfrac{1}{18} \approx 0.056. The baseline has \sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2 = \tfrac{14}{3} (with \bar y = \tfrac83), hence R^2 = 1 - \tfrac{1/6}{14/3} = \tfrac{27}{28} \approx 0.964.

Now the same computation in Python.

X_toy = np.array([[1.0, 0.0],
                  [1.0, 1.0],
                  [1.0, 2.0]])
y_toy = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 4.0])

A = X_toy.T @ X_toy
b = X_toy.T @ y_toy
print("X^T X =\n", A)
print("X^T y =", b)

w_toy = np.linalg.solve(A, b)                   # solves the normal equations
print("w     =", w_toy, "  (expected 7/6 and 3/2:", 7 / 6, 3 / 2, ")")

y_hat = X_toy @ w_toy
r = y_toy - y_hat
print("y_hat =", y_hat)
print("r     =", r)
print("X^T r =", np.round(X_toy.T @ r, 12), "  <- orthogonality of the residual")
print("MSE   =", np.mean(r ** 2), "  (expected 1/18 =", 1 / 18, ")")

sst = np.sum((y_toy - y_toy.mean()) ** 2)
print("R^2   =", 1 - np.sum(r ** 2) / sst, "  (expected 27/28 =", 27 / 28, ")")

records.content:
The three samples of the toy problem live in \mathbb{R}^3. The two columns of \mathbf{X} span a plane (the column space). The vector \mathbf{y} is not on the plane; its projection \hat{\mathbf{y}} is the closest point of the plane, and the residual \mathbf{r} is perpendicular to it. For the picture we keep the matrix \mathbf{X} of Worked example 1.2 but use the targets \mathbf{y} = (3, 1, 4)^\top, whose fit is worse: this makes the residual long enough to be seen. The right panel shows the same picture looking along the plane, so that the plane appears as a line and the right angle between the residual and the plane becomes visible.

# Figure 1.2 — geometry of least squares for a small example
def figure_1_2():
    import numpy as np
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    # same matrix X as in Worked example 1.2, but with targets y = (3, 1, 4):
    # the fit is worse, so the residual is long enough to be seen clearly
    X = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
    y = np.array([3.0, 1.0, 4.0])
    w = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
    y_hat = X @ w

    # a direction perpendicular to the plane: the cross product of the two columns of X.
    # Looking at the plane "edge-on" means looking along a direction orthogonal to it.
    normal = np.cross(X[:, 0], X[:, 1])                   # = (1, -2, 1)
    azim_edge_on = np.degrees(np.arctan2(-normal[0], normal[1]))   # azimuth whose view direction is in the plane
    # view direction for (elev=0, azim): (cos azim, sin azim, 0). We need it orthogonal to `normal`.
    assert abs(np.dot([np.cos(np.radians(azim_edge_on)), np.sin(np.radians(azim_edge_on)), 0], normal)) < 1e-9

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 5.4))
    views = [(14, -35, "General view"), (0, azim_edge_on, "Edge-on view: the plane is seen as a line")]
    for k, (elev, azim, title) in enumerate(views, start=1):
        ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, k, projection="3d")

        # the plane spanned by the two columns of X (the column space)
        s, t = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-0.8, 1.8, 14), np.linspace(-0.8, 1.8, 14))
        plane = s[..., None] * X[:, 0] + t[..., None] * X[:, 1]
        ax.plot_surface(plane[..., 0], plane[..., 1], plane[..., 2], alpha=0.18, color=SKY, linewidth=0)
        ax.plot_wireframe(plane[..., 0], plane[..., 1], plane[..., 2], color=SKY, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0.4)

        origin = np.zeros(3)
        for start, end, color, label, ls in [
            (origin, y, "black", r"$\mathbf{y}$ (targets)", "-"),
            (origin, y_hat, BLUE, r"$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ (projection)", "-"),
            (y_hat, y, VERMILION, r"$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ (residual)", "--"),
        ]:
            ax.plot(*zip(start, end), color=color, linewidth=2.4, linestyle=ls, label=label)
            ax.scatter(*end, color=color, s=24)

        ax.set_xlabel("sample 1")
        ax.set_ylabel("sample 2")
        ax.set_zlabel("sample 3")
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
        ax.set_xticks([0, 1, 2, 3])
        ax.set_yticks([-1, 0, 1, 2, 3])
        ax.set_zticks([0, 2, 4])
        ax.set_box_aspect((1, 1, 1))
        ax.view_init(elev=elev, azim=azim)
        if k == 1:
            ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
    fig.suptitle("Least squares: orthogonal projection onto the column space", y=0.98)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

figure_1_2()

We now fit a line to the Diabetes data, using a single feature, the body mass index. We compute the solution in three ways: with the normal equations, with np.linalg.lstsq, and with scikit-learn’s LinearRegression. They should agree.

Pitfall

Writing np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y is mathematically correct but numerically fragile: the matrix \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} can be nearly singular, and inverting it amplifies rounding errors. Solve the linear system (np.linalg.solve) or, better, use np.linalg.lstsq, which relies on the SVD of \mathbf{X} and also copes with rank-deficient matrices. We will understand why in Chapter 13. Exercise 1.10 shows a failure case.

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

bmi = X_diab["bmi"].to_numpy()
A_bmi = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(bmi), bmi])          # add the column of ones

w_normal = np.linalg.solve(A_bmi.T @ A_bmi, A_bmi.T @ y)   # 1) normal equations
w_lstsq = np.linalg.lstsq(A_bmi, y, rcond=None)[0]         # 2) SVD-based solver
sk = LinearRegression().fit(bmi.reshape(-1, 1), y)         # 3) scikit-learn

print("normal equations  :", w_normal.round(4))
print("np.linalg.lstsq   :", w_lstsq.round(4))
print("scikit-learn      :", np.array([sk.intercept_, sk.coef_[0]]).round(4))
print("all three agree   :", np.allclose(w_normal, w_lstsq) and np.allclose(w_normal, [sk.intercept_, sk.coef_[0]]))

y_hat_bmi = A_bmi @ w_lstsq
mse_bmi = np.mean((y - y_hat_bmi) ** 2)
r2_bmi = 1 - np.sum((y - y_hat_bmi) ** 2) / np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)
print(f"\nMSE: {mse_bmi:.1f}  (baseline: {mse_baseline:.1f})")
print(f"R^2: {r2_bmi:.3f}")
print(f"sum of residuals: {np.sum(y - y_hat_bmi):.2e}   <- zero, as shown in the theory")



The slope says that, on this data set, one extra unit of BMI goes with about ten extra units of disease progression. The fit explains roughly a third of the variance of y (the exact R^2 is printed above): clearly better than the baseline, but far from perfect.

# Figure 1.3 — the least-squares line and its residuals
def figure_1_3():
    import numpy as np
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes

    d = load_diabetes(as_frame=True, scaled=False)
    x, t = d.data["bmi"].to_numpy(), d.target.to_numpy()
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])
    w = np.linalg.lstsq(A, t, rcond=None)[0]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.4))
    ax.scatter(x, t, s=16, color=BLUE, alpha=0.55, edgecolor="none", label="patients")

    # residuals of a few randomly chosen points, to make the "errors" visible
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    for i in rng.choice(len(x), size=25, replace=False):
        ax.plot([x[i], x[i]], [t[i], w[0] + w[1] * x[i]], color=VERMILION, linewidth=1, alpha=0.8)
    ax.plot([], [], color=VERMILION, linewidth=1, label="residuals (25 shown)")

    xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 100)
    ax.plot(xs, w[0] + w[1] * xs, color="black", linewidth=2, label="least-squares line")
    ax.axhline(t.mean(), color=GREEN, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5, label="baseline: the mean")
    ax.set_xlabel("body mass index (bmi)")
    ax.set_ylabel("disease progression after one year")
    ax.set_title("Diabetes data: one feature, one line")
    ax.legend()
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

The R^2 rose, as it must: adding columns can only enlarge the column space and bring the projection closer to \mathbf{y}. But the R^2 computed on the data used to fit the model is an optimistic number. The next section explains why, and what to do about it.

records.content:
What we really care about is not the loss on the training samples, but the loss on future samples drawn from the same source. Call \mathcal{D} the (unknown) distribution that generates the data. The quantity of interest is the expected riskR(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y) \sim \mathcal{D}}\bigl[\ell\bigl(y, f(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\bigr],

which we cannot compute because \mathcal{D} is unknown. The empirical risk \hat{R}_S(f) on the training set is a biased estimate of it, because f was chosen precisely to make \hat{R}_S(f) small. The standard remedy is to keep some samples aside:

the training set is used to fit the model;

the test set is never used for fitting, only to estimate R(f) at the very end.

records.content:
A model that is too rigid cannot capture the pattern in the data: underfitting. A model that is too flexible also adapts to the random fluctuations of the training sample, which will not repeat on new data: overfitting. Flexibility can be controlled in many ways; here we use the simplest one, the degree of a polynomial. We fit f(x) = w_0 + w_1 x + \dots + w_m x^m to the BMI/progression data. This is still linear least squares: the “features” are 1, x, x^2, \dots, x^m, and the normal equations are the same as before.

To make the effect visible we train on only 30 patients and test on the remaining 412. (With few training examples, flexible models overfit sooner; this is a general phenomenon.) The right panel repeats the experiment on 300 different random splits and reports the median error, which is more reliable than a single split.

# Figure 1.4 — fits of increasing flexibility, and training vs. test error
import numpy as np
from numpy.polynomial import polynomial as P
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

N_TRAIN, MAX_DEG = 30, 10

def fit_and_score(z_tr, y_tr, z_te, y_te, degree):
    """Least squares on the features 1, z, ..., z^degree; returns the coefficients and the two MSEs."""
    coef = P.polyfit(z_tr, y_tr, degree)
    mse = lambda zz, yy: np.mean((yy - P.polyval(zz, coef)) ** 2)
    return coef, mse(z_tr, y_tr), mse(z_te, y_te)

def figure_1_4():
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    d = load_diabetes(as_frame=True, scaled=False)
    bmi, target = d.data["bmi"].to_numpy(), d.target.to_numpy()
    z = (bmi - bmi.mean()) / bmi.std()          # standardize the feature for numerical stability

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4))

    # Left: one particular split, three polynomial degrees
    z_tr, z_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(z, target, train_size=N_TRAIN, random_state=3)
    axes[0].scatter(z_te, y_te, s=10, color="0.75", label="test patients (412)")
    axes[0].scatter(z_tr, y_tr, s=36, color=BLUE, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6, zorder=3,
                    label=f"training patients ({N_TRAIN})")
    grid = np.linspace(z.min(), z.max(), 300)
    for degree, color, style in [(1, GREEN, "-"), (3, ORANGE, "--"), (9, VERMILION, "-")]:
        coef, mse_tr, mse_te = fit_and_score(z_tr, y_tr, z_te, y_te, degree)
        axes[0].plot(grid, P.polyval(grid, coef), color=color, linestyle=style, linewidth=2,
                     label=f"degree {degree}: train MSE {mse_tr:.0f}, test MSE {mse_te:.3g}")
    axes[0].set_ylim(target.min() - 40, target.max() + 40)
    axes[0].set_xlabel("standardized bmi")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("disease progression")
    axes[0].set_title("One split: flexible fits chase the noise")
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")

    # Right: median errors over many random splits
    errs = np.zeros((300, MAX_DEG + 1, 2))
    for s in range(300):
        z_tr, z_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(z, target, train_size=N_TRAIN, random_state=s)
        for degree in range(MAX_DEG + 1):
            _, errs[s, degree, 0], errs[s, degree, 1] = fit_and_score(z_tr, y_tr, z_te, y_te, degree)
    med = np.median(errs, axis=0)
    degrees = np.arange(MAX_DEG + 1)
    axes[1].plot(degrees, med[:, 0], "o-", color=BLUE, label="training error")
    axes[1].plot(degrees, med[:, 1], "s--", color=VERMILION, label="test error")
    axes[1].axhline(np.var(target), color=GREEN, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5, label="baseline (variance of y)")
    axes[1].set_yscale("log")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("polynomial degree (model flexibility)")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("mean squared error (log scale)")
    axes[1].set_title("Median over 300 random splits")
    axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    return med

med = figure_1_4()
best = int(np.argmin(med[:, 1]))
print(f"Degree with the smallest median test error: {best}")
print("Training error never increases with the degree (nested models, same data):",
      bool(np.all(np.diff(med[:, 0]) <= 1e-9)))





Read the right panel from left to right.

Training error goes down all the way: a more flexible model can always fit the training sample at least as well (the models are nested). On its own it would tell us to pick the most complex model.

Test error is high at degree 0 (underfitting: the constant ignores the input; it is the baseline), is lowest at a low degree, and then explodes (overfitting): the high-degree polynomials oscillate wildly between and beyond the training points, as the left panel shows.

The gap between the two curves is the price of optimism of the training error. This U-shaped test curve is the central picture of the bias–variance trade-off, which we study in depth in Chapter 4, and the reason why Chapter 5 is entirely devoted to choosing the model complexity in a principled way.

Key idea

Never judge a model by its error on the data used to fit it. Keep a test set aside, use it once, at the end, and report that number.

The data set (Street, Wolberg and Mangasarian, 1993) contains 569 digitized images of fine needle aspirates of breast masses. For each image, 30 numerical features describe the cell nuclei (radius, texture, area, and so on), and the label says whether the mass is malignant or benign. It is bundled with scikit-learn. This is a teaching example: the point is the method, not medical advice.

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

bc = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
X_bc, y_bc = bc.data, bc.target
print("X shape:", X_bc.shape)
print("classes:", dict(zip(bc.target_names.tolist(), np.bincount(y_bc).tolist())))
print("\nThe features live on very different scales:")
X_bc.describe().loc[["mean", "std"]].T.iloc[[0, 3, 4]].round(3)





Two observations before modeling. First, the classes are not perfectly balanced, so a trivial classifier that always answers “benign” already reaches a respectable accuracy: this is our baseline for classification, the analogue of the mean in regression. Second, mean area is of the order of hundreds, while mean smoothness is about 0.1: features on such different scales will be a problem for methods based on distances.
